title: Rates and reversibility of CO2 hydrogenation on Cu-based catalysts
abstract: Kinetics of reaction pathways involved in the conversion of CO2 to methanol and CO on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 are resolved using in situ chemical titration, steady-state kinetic measurements, and mathematical formalisms for reversibility to probe salient species governing methanol selectivity and yield during CO2 hydrogenation. Across a range of H2:CO2 = 1:1 to H2:CO2 = 80.5:1, active site density determined from in situ chlorine uptake remained invariant; hence, observed trends in rates can be interpreted as only arising from reaction kinetics and not from changing active site density. Kinetic and thermodynamic contributions to rates are decoupled to evaluate forward and reverse rates of methanol synthesis and reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) reactions. These kinetic analyses show that the forward rates of methanol synthesis exhibit persistent first order dependence on hydrogen pressure and are inhibited by water more significantly than the forward rates of RWGS. In contrast, the reverse rates of methanol synthesis and RWGS are both inhibited by H2. Consequently, without any modifications to the Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst formulation, methanol selectivity can be increased to > 80 % by increasing inlet H2 partial pressure and methanol yield can be enhanced by ∼ 20 % by adding water adsorbents even under conditions far from equilibrium. The kinetic treatments presented herein demonstrate a dearth of H* species during catalysis, provide thermodynamic constraints precluding sequential RWGS and CO hydrogenation as the pathway for methanol synthesis, reveal PH2 and PH2O as salient in determining methanol selectivity and yield by impacting both the forward and reverse rates of CO2 hydrogenation on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3, and explicate the fundamentals of novel sorption-enhanced methanol synthesis, which not only alleviates equilibrium constraints but also alters the intrinsic rate at which the system approaches equilibrium.

CO2 hydrogenation results in the production of CH3OH, H2O, and CO through competing methanol synthesis (Eq. (1)) and reverse water–gas shift (RWGS; Eq. (2)) pathways, thereby reducing methanol selectivity during CO2 hydrogenation in reference to CO-to-CH3OH processes (Eq. (3)). While growing efforts to engineer novel materials that proffer enhanced methanol selectivity have undeniably led to advancements in catalyst design, comparatively fewer studies have been devoted to examining salient gas phase and surface species that determine rates and selectivity of CO2 hydrogenation even on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3, the conventional catalyst formulation for methanol synthesis from syngas mixtures. Among studies aimed at elucidating the reaction mechanism, techniques such as infrared spectroscopy, kinetic isotopic effect, transient kinetic measurements, and density functional theory calculations have been employed to propose the involvement of either formate or carboxylate as the reactive intermediate for CO2 hydrogenation. The lack of definitive evidence for the reactive intermediates and their reactivity, however, calls into question the network connectivity between the three possible reactions (Eqs. (1)–(3)). (1) C O 2 + 3 H 2 ⇄ C H 3 O H + H 2 O (2) C O 2 + H 2 ⇄ C O + H 2 O (3) CO + 2 H 2 ⇄ C H 3 O H

A corollary to the undefined kinetics of CO2 hydrogenation is the identity and number of active sites on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalysts which has also eluded consensus. Specifically, the role of ZnO in enhancing methanol selectivity relative to that obtained with Cu/SiO2 or Cu/Al2O3 catalysts is still in debate. Research efforts have focused not only on whether ZnO alters the morphology of Cu particles or engenders additional active sites but also on the effect and extent of ZnO reduction. Notwithstanding the careful use of a variety of analytical and computational techniques including transmission electron microscopy, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, ex situ titration, in situ chemical pulsing, and thermodynamic calculations, the results appear inconclusive; Cu with fully reduced Zn centers (Cu/Zn alloy), Cu with partially reduced Znδ+ centers, ZnOx overlayer on Cu, and ZnO-Cu interface on inverse ZnO/Cu catalysts each have been proposed as the active site. Laudenschleger et al. have attempted to rationalize all proposed active motifs through the slow oxidation of Zn centers over time. On the other hand, Grunwaldt et al. and Tu et al. have suggested that the extent of Cu/Zn interactions can increase with increasing H2-to-H2O or CO-to-CO2 ratios based on characterization of Cu/ZnO and Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalysts using a combination of X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy and in situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. These dynamic changes, if prevalent, greatly hinder kinetic analyses of rates and selectivity as rate measurements necessarily reflect a convolution of changing active site density and changing chemical activity of the species present.

From a thermodynamic standpoint, the negative entropic change associated with methanol synthesis via CO2 hydrogenation imposes severe equilibrium limitations despite its exothermic nature, further hampering the elucidation of the intrinsic kinetic behaviors as observed net rates of reaction can include both kinetic and thermodynamic contributions. While this complexity can typically be mitigated by narrowing the scope of study to irreversible regimes where the system is far from equilibrium and the reaction appears irreversible, such practices not only restrict the reaction conditions to ones that are often impractical but also overlook decades of development in reaction rate theories specifically for reversible reactions. Indeed, formalisms such as de Donder’s inequality (Eq. (4); where A i , r i , and z i are the chemical affinity, net rate, and reversibility of the i th elementary step) provide relationships relating rates and reversibility of reactions that can proffer additional insights into reaction network connectivity otherwise unavailable from the evaluation of apparent reaction orders alone. (4) A i r i ≥ 0 ⇒ i f r i ≥ 0 t h e n A i ≥ 0 a n d z i ≤ 1 Exemplary studies of the application of de Donder’s relations and reversibility include the work of Holstein and Boudart, which demonstrated that cyclic reactions are disallowed based on considerations of chemical affinities, and, more recently, the work of Razdan et al., which reaffirmed the single-path reaction mechanism of methane dehydroaromatization by consistently showing that all relevant reversibility values are less than unity and underscored the distinction between rates and reversibility in a plug flow reactor, with rates being length-averaged and reversibility being instantaneous.

Herein, we combine in situ chemical titrations, steady-state kinetic measurements, and mathematical formalisms grounded in thermodynamics to elucidate the reaction kinetics and, pursuant to this analysis, improve the methanol selectivity during CO2 hydrogenation on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 by identifying species that influence the forward and reverse rates of methanol synthesis and RWGS. Site density, enumerated through chlorine uptake, remains invariant with changing H2:CO2 ratio, illustrating that rate measurements reflect intrinsic kinetic behaviors and are not influenced by changes in site density. We then leverage kinetic measurements under both irreversible and reversible regimes to evaluate the net, forward, and reverse rates of reaction by decoupling kinetic and thermodynamic contributions to rates. These results, in conjunction with thermodynamic constraints afforded by de Donder’s relations, show that methanol synthesis and RWGS proceed through a branching reaction pathway involving distinct intermediates such that unidirectional forward and reverse rates of the two reactions exhibit different dependencies on species partial pressures. Forward and reverse rates, unlike net rates, are devoid of thermodynamic effects and reflect only the underlying kinetic contributions to rates. To this end, H2 and H2O are identified as the salient species governing the unidirectional forward rate of methanol synthesis. Without altering the catalyst formulation, increasing H2 partial pressures in the reaction feed and incorporating water adsorbents in the catalyst bed to decrease H2O partial pressure can enhance methanol selectivity and yield during CO2 hydrogenation on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3.

Commercially available Cu-based methanol synthesis catalyst (Alfa Aesar; product 45776; lot X03F006) and Cu/Al2O3 catalyst (13 wt%; Sigma-Aldrich; product 417971; batch MKCR8846) were used for steady-state rate measurements. SEM-EDS (Hitachi; SU8230) showed that the commercial Cu-based catalyst is a conventional Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalyst with minor magnesium promoter concentrations, in agreement with the product specification provided by the manufacturer (Sec. S1; Supporting Information (SI)). Prior to use, both catalysts were crushed, pressed, and sieved to obtain aggregates that are 180–250 μm in diameter. Catalyst samples (0.005–0.081 g) were first charged into a glass-lined stainless-steel reactor (1/4″ O.D.; Trajan Scientific) with a quartz rod (1/8″ O.D.) and quartz wool plug as support. Sand (Acros Organics; acid-washed with 2 M HNO3 overnight and treated in flowing dry air (Parker Balston; HPZA-18000) at 1273 K for 10 h) was subsequently added in a 1:10 dilution by mass for Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 (catalyst:sand = 1:10 by mass) and 1:1 dilution by mass for Cu/Al2O3 (catalyst:sand = 1:1 by mass) to mitigate thermal gradients due to the exothermicity of reaction. After vigorously shaking the reactor to ensure proper mixing, a quartz wool plug and quartz rod was then added to secure the catalyst bed. The entire reactor setup was heated resistively (National Element Inc.; FA120V120), monitored by a thermocouple (Omega; TJ36-CAXL-020U-12-SMPW-M) threaded around the outer wall near the catalyst bed, and controlled by a PID controller (Watlow; Series 96). For reactions at integral conversion and reversibility, a second thermocouple was threaded around the outer wall of the reactor near the end of the catalyst bed due to the increased bed length; the maximum axial temperature gradient was determined to be less than 4 K at CO2 fractional conversions below 0.09.

Flow rates of He (Airgas; UHP; 99.999 %), CO2 (Airgas; Research Grade; 99.999 %), H2 (Airgas; UHP; 99.999 %), and/or Ar (Airgas, Research Grade; 99.9997 %) during pretreatment and reaction were controlled by mass-flow controllers (Brooks Instrument; SLA5850). Henceforth, the minimum purities of gases are as reported above unless otherwise noted. Gas carrier lines, held at ca. 353 K to prevent condensation, and the catalyst bed, kept at ambient temperature, were first purged using an inert gas (He or Ar; 3.7 × 10−5 mol s−1) under ambient pressure for at least 6 h. The temperature and pressure of gas lines are monitored with a thermocouple (Omega; TJ36-CAXL-020U-12-SMPW-M) and pressure transducer (Omega; PX109-1KG5V), respectively. The catalyst sample was then pretreated under a 5 % H2 stream with He or Ar as balance (8.0 × 10−5 mol s−1; ambient pressure) at 523 K (0.03 K s−1 from ambient temperature) and held for 2 h. Reduction of the catalyst during pretreatment was confirmed with the evolution of water (m/z = 18) measured with an online mass spectrometer (MKS; Cirrus 2; Sec. S2; SI). After pretreatment, the reactor was purged and pressurized (Enpro; 26–1700 series regulator) to the reaction pressure with an inert gas (He or Ar; 10–40 bar) while holding the temperature at 523 K. Reaction was initiated by introducing the reaction mixture (CO2 + H2 + He + Ar; 6.9 × 10−5–4.2 × 10−4 mol s−1) with the desired mole fractions at the desired total pressure. Effluent compositions were determined using both a flame ionization detector and a thermal conductivity detector configured on a gas chromatograph (GC; Agilent; 7890A) equipped with PLOT-U and CP-Molsieve 5A columns. Relative response factors were obtained by introducing gas mixtures across a range of known concentrations along with Ar serving as the internal standard. Contributions from mass and heat transport were ruled out experimentally based on comparable rates obtained with smaller catalyst aggregates (125–180 μm in diameter) and on catalyst beds with and without sand diluent (Sec. S3; SI).

Based on the measured effluent flow rates, CO2 conversion to methanol and CO were calculated as (5a) X C O 2 → C H 3 O H = F C H 3 O H F C O 2 + F C H 3 O H + F CO (5b) X C O 2 → C O = F CO F C O 2 + F C H 3 O H + F CO where F i is the effluent molar flow rate of species i . Total CO2 conversion and methanol selectivity were defined as X C O 2 = X C O 2 → C H 3 O H + X C O 2 → C O and S M e O H = X C O 2 → C H 3 O H / X C O 2 = F C H 3 O H / ( F C H 3 O H + F CO ) , respectively. Trace methyl formate and dimethyl ether were detected in certain cases, but the concentrations of these species were estimated to be more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of methanol and CO based on the observed GC peak areas. Hence, these species were neglected in Equation (5). Equilibrium constants at the reaction temperature (523 K) were determined based on temperature-corrected standard-state enthalpies and entropies (Sec. S4; SI). Due to limitations of the employed GC system in detecting H2 and H2O with high accuracy and the strong sensitivity of Equation (6) to F H 2 and F H 2 O , these flow rates were instead calculated based on inlet H2 flow rate, F C H 3 O H , and F CO using the appropriate reaction stoichiometry (Eqs. (1) and (2)). This approximation was only employed for the determination of Z o v ; F H 2 and F H 2 O as measured were reported in all other cases where these values are relevant.

N2O reactive frontal chromatography (N2O-RFC) was employed to enumerate the number of exposed Cu atoms ex situ following methods reported previously. Immediately after pretreatment, the furnace set point was reduced to 363 K and the catalyst was held in flowing He (7.4 × 10−5 mol s−1) for at least 2 h to allow temperature to stabilize. To initiate titration, 1 % N2O/He (3.0 × 10−5 mol s−1; Airgas; certified mixture from VLSI Grade N2O and UHP He) was introduced with Ar (1.5 × 10−5 mol s−1) as an inert tracer. An additional 7.4 × 10−5 mol s−1 of CO (Airgas; semiconductor grade; 99.997 %) was added to the effluent as an external standard for analysis using an online mass spectrometer (MKS; Cirrus 2). Relative response factors were obtained daily using the final signals of N2O, Ar, and CO after titration reached completion.

In situ chemical titration of Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 was performed with methylene chloride (Sigma-Aldrich; HPLC Plus; ≥ 99.9 %), a known poison for Cu catalysts, injected and vaporized at elevated pressures with a 20 cm3 stainless-steel syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus; PHD Ultra). With rates at steady state under a reactant stream without CH2Cl2 (desired CO2 and H2 partial pressures + 5 bar He; 1.1 × 10−4–2.9 × 10−4 mol s−1; 523 K), a second titrant stream with the same CO2 and H2 pressures as the reactant stream, 1.5 kPa CH2Cl2, and Ar balance was stabilized in bypass such that the reactant and titrant streams are at the same total pressure and flow rate. CH2Cl2 chemical titration was initiated by switching the reactant stream to bypass and the titrant stream to the reactor. In all cases, variations in total pressure before and after the switch were visually confirmed from pressure readouts to be less than 1 %. Effluent composition was quantified by both gas chromatography and online mass spectrometry (described above). Each consumed CH2Cl2 was assumed to fully decompose and deposit two Cl adatoms. Each Cl adatom was assumed to titrate one active site. Furthermore, titration was confirmed to be irreversible as returning the titrant stream to bypass and the reactant stream to the reactor did not restore any activity in methanol synthesis and RWGS.

Molecular sieve 3A (Sigma-Aldrich; treated in flowing dry air (Parker Balston; HPZA-18000; 1.5 × 10−4 mol s−1) at 823 K (0.02 K s−1 from ambient temperature) for 4 h; crushed, pressed, and sieved to 180–250 μm in diameter) was physically mixed with Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 (Alfa Aesar; prepared as described above) in a 1:10 ratio by mass (catalyst:molecular sieve 3A = 1:10 by mass) to evaluate the effect of water abstraction during catalysis. Mixtures (330 mg) were placed into the same reactor setup as described in Section 2.1 without additional sand diluent and pretreated under 5 % H2/He (8.0 × 10−5 mol s−1; ambient pressure) at 523 K (0.03 K s−1 from ambient temperature) and held for 2 h. The reactor was then flushed with He (7.4 × 10−5 mol s−1; ambient pressure), cooled to 423 K (0.3 K s−1 from 523 K), and held for 10 h to facilitate the desorption of residual water while mitigating catalyst sintering. The catalyst bed was subsequently heated to 503 K (0.03 K s−1 from 423 K) and pressurized to 60 bar (Enpro; 26–1700 series regulator) with CO2, Ar (30 % CO2/Ar; Airgas; Certified Standard from Research Grade CO2 and Ar), and He in a CO2:He:Ar = 1:3:2.3 molar ratio to establish internal standards prior to the introduction of H2 for reaction. A lower temperature and higher total pressure were employed in comparison to those for steady-state kinetic measurements (Sec. 2.1) to facilitate water uptake. Reaction was initiated by introducing the reaction mixture (CO2:H2:Ar = 1:2.9:2.3; 8.9 × 10−5 mol s−1), and the effluent composition was analyzed by gas chromatography as described above (Sec. 2.1) in conjunction with an online mass spectrometer (MKS; Cirrus 1) for temporal resolution.

As previously suggested by Beck et al. based on operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy and in situ time-resolved X-ray diffraction, Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 samples under methanol synthesis conditions may differ from those immediately after the reductive pretreatment. Furthermore, the dynamic restructuring schemes suggested by Grunwaldt et al. and Tu et al. call into question the typical approach of normalizing measured reaction rates by a site density assessed ex situ and by a site density that is invariant with process conditions. Herein, we introduced methylene chloride as an irreversible chemical titrant to achieve in situ quantification of active site density in addition to N2O-RFC (Sec. S5; SI). As shown in Fig. 1 , the introduction of 1.5 kPa methylene chloride led to an immediate decrease in the evolution rates of methanol, water, and CO, which do not return upon removal of methylene chloride from the feed stream. The decrease in rates is initially linear with the amount of Cl deposition, suggesting that methylene chloride is poisoning the relevant sites by stoichiometrically depositing Cl adatoms. The eventual deviation from a linear relationship may be explained by hydrodynamic effects, unselective titration, or more complex processes such as the formation of CuCl2 that undergoes sintering or the generation of ZnCl2 that overcoats Cu nanoparticles. Accordingly, as conveyed by Afrin and Bollini, we utilize and extrapolate the initial linear decrease in water evolution rate, which reflects the sum of methanol synthesis and RWGS rates by stoichiometry (Eqs. (1) and (2)), to quantify the site density for Cl adsorption devoid of more complex phenomena (Table 1 ). Errors in site densities assessed by CH2Cl2 titration were approximated based on four additional repeat experiments at H2:CO2 = 1:1, which was conducted at the lowest total pressure, resulting in the largest relative pressure swing and syringe flow instability upon the onset of titration (Table 2 ).

Regardless of the specificity for Cl to titrate Cu, Zn, or, in all likelihood, both, the results demonstrate that the total Cl uptake is invariant across H2:CO2 = 1:1, H2:CO2 = 5:1, and H2:CO2 = 80.5:1 molar ratios. Any changes in the extent of Cu-Zn interactions, whether through processes such as Cu wetting/non-wetting on ZnO or formation of a CuZn alloy, would inevitably lead to changes in the number of exposed Cu and Zn, thereby altering the total Cl uptake. The data in Table 1 thus show that there is no significant generation of Cu or Zn centers relevant for CO2 hydrogenation at higher H2 partial pressures during reaction (Table 1). A constant Cl uptake can manifest if the generation of Zn atoms stoichiometrically replaces surface Cu atoms precisely as the H2-to-CO2 ratio changes. This, however, is not a valid explanation as we show, in the following section, that RWGS rates exhibit zeroth-order dependence on PH2 (Fig. 2 ), and RWGS activity has been previously demonstrated to vary linearly with Cu metal surface area on Cu/ZnO and Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 catalysts. In other words, the total Cl uptake is invariant because both the number of Cu and Zn centers are largely unchanged when changing H2:CO2 ratio from 1:1 to 80.5:1.

On a freshly pretreated catalyst sample, site density was measured with ex situ CH2Cl2 titration to be only 1.6 relative to the number of exposed Cu as determined from N2O-RFC (Sec. S7; SI). The higher Cl uptake under working condition suggests that Cu nanoparticles can redisperse or that additional active centers (e.g., reduced Zn centers) can, in fact, be generated upon introduction of reaction feed, which has higher H2 pressures than the pretreatment stream. The invariance of Cl uptake during reaction with changing H2:CO2 ratio and H2 partial pressure therefore does not preclude the reduction of ZnO and complex Cu-Zn interactions [22–24,26–31] but simply demonstrates that observed trends in reaction rate and selectivity are derived solely from the underlying reaction kinetics. In the following sections, we leverage this result and accordingly normalize all reported rate measurements by a single value of site density measured from in situ titration (Table 1; average site density) to elicit intrinsic kinetic information.

As shown in Fig. 2, an increase in H2 partial pressure at a constant CO2 partial pressure linearly increases methanol synthesis site-time yield and does not influence RWGS site-time yield, in agreement with previous studies. Similar apparent reaction orders were observed on Cu/Al2O3 catalysts despite reaction on Cu/Al2O3 exhibiting a lower selectivity toward methanol, congruent with the fact that changes in rates do not arise from a change in active site density stemming from ZnO reduction (Sec. S8; SI). The first order dependence of methanol synthesis and zeroth order dependence of RWGS in PH2 prescribe a unique significance to H2 in modulating methanol yield and selectivity during CO2 hydrogenation. In the case of PCO2 = 0.25 bar, increasing PH2 from 0.25 bar to 25 bar increases methanol selectivity by more than an order of magnitude, attaining methanol selectivities near 80 % (Fig. 2b). From a kinetic standpoint, the observed H2 dependencies underscore a difference in rate-determining steps of methanol synthesis and RWGS, where the methanol synthesis rate-determining step should involve two additional H* species. The persistent first order PH2 dependence even at PCO2 = 0.25 bar (with H2:CO2 ratio reaching 100:1) where it is expected that the surface coverage of the CO2-derived intermediate is low (Fig. 3 ) additionally demonstrates that there is a dearth of H* species during catalysis at all conditions. Increasing PH2 appears to always be able to deposit more H* species and selectively enhance methanol synthesis rate over RWGS rate. Potential explanations for the persistent first order dependence in PH2 could include: (i) the dissociative adsorption equilibrium constant for H2 is sufficiently low, (ii) CO2-derived surface species rapidly scavenge surface H* species to form other H-containing species, and (iii) the relevant surface intermediate for catalysis inherently has more than two H atoms.

In contrast to the effects of PH2, both methanol synthesis and RWGS rates appear to follow Langmuir-type saturation kinetics with respect to PCO2 at a constant PH2 (Fig. 3), also in agreement with previously established microkinetic models for CO2 hydrogenation. Accordingly, the trends in Fig. 3 follow the form (7) r = a P C O 2 1 + b P C O 2 where a and b are determined using a least-square fit. The observed CO2 effect more importantly demonstrates that methanol selectivity remains largely invariant with CO2 partial pressure with slight deviations only occurring at PCO2 below 2 bar.

While the evaluation of apparent reaction orders is undoubtedly a fruitful and perhaps predominant approach to evince possible reaction mechanisms, validation of purported reaction pathways often requires derivation of rate expressions, which, in turn, requires assumptions regarding the reaction network connectivity. In what follows, we instead leverage the reversible nature of CO2 hydrogenation to invoke formalisms grounded in thermodynamics and reversibility. These relations not only provide stringent requirements on network connectivity between methanol synthesis and RWGS (Sec. 3.3) but also enable us to deconvolute the above observations on net rates of CO2 hydrogenation into those for the unidirectional forward and reverse rates (Sec. 3.4).

To discern whether methanol is formed directly from CO2 (Eq. (1)) or from a sequential RWGS (Eq. (2)) and CO hydrogenation (Eq. (3)) pathway (Scheme 1 ), we utilize two thermodynamic constraints for reversible reactions: (i) the effective reversibility of an overall reaction is the product of the reversibility of its constituent elementary steps regardless of the network connectivity (Eq. (8)), and (ii) the reversibility of each constitutive elementary step in a closed catalytic cycle must be less than unity for the reaction to proceed in the forward direction per de Donder’s inequality (Eq. (4)). Consequently, a sequential RWGS and CO hydrogenation pathway for methanol synthesis requires the effective reversibility of methanol synthesis to be lower than that of RWGS (Eq. (9b)). (8) Z e f f = ∏ i = s t e p s N z i (9a) Z e f f , C O 2 → C H 3 O H = Z e f f , C O 2 → C O Z e f f , C O → C H 3 O H (9b) Z e f f , C O 2 → C H 3 O H ≤ Z e f f , C O 2 → C O s i n c e 0 ≤ Z e f f , C O → C H 3 O H ≤ 1 In the case of CO2 hydrogenation, we surmise that all elementary steps have unity stoichiometric numbers except for H2 adsorption and activation, which are likely equilibrated. This, in turn, enables us to equate effective and overall reversibilities and restate the above constraint using instead the overall reversibilities of methanol synthesis and RWGS, which are readily assessed based on experimental measurements (Eq. (6)).

At each condition shown in Fig. 2a, however, the calculated overall reversibility for methanol synthesis is higher than that of RWGS (Fig. 4 ), showing that methanol synthesis is more equilibrium limited than RWGS. More critically, these reversibility values contradict the requirement for any postulated sequential RWGS and CO hydrogenation pathway for the generation of methanol. Indeed, explicit calculation of the overall reversibility of CO hydrogenation to methanol (Sec. S9; SI) consistently yields values greater than unity; that is to say, CO hydrogenation to methanol cannot occur at a positive net rate. The CO2-to-CO-to-CH3OH sequential pathway is therefore thermodynamically forbidden under the conditions presented herein. While methanol can dehydrogenate to form CO, the observed apparent H2 reaction orders where CH3OH partial pressure can be increased significantly with increasing PH2 while CO partial pressure remains unchanged indicate this pathway should occur at insignificant rates (Fig. 2). Together, the above reversibility-based arguments show that the reaction network of CO2 hydrogenation is branched, with CO and CH3OH stemming from distinct pathways involving different intermediates (Scheme 2 ). With this in mind, we next address the convolution of kinetic and thermodynamic driving forces, observed especially at low H2 partial pressures (Fig. 4), and reevaluate the reported net rates in terms of their constitutive forward and reverse components, which, unlike net rates, reflect solely the kinetic contributions to rates free of thermodynamic effects stemming from the reversibility of reaction.

Differential conversion and irreversible conditions, while desirable for the mitigation of concentration gradients and equilibrium limitations, restrict kinetic analyses to a limited range of process conditions that are often impractical. We here focus instead on reaction rates at integral conditions and employ appropriate mathematical formalisms to simultaneously extract information on both the forward and reverse unidirectional rates specific to the methanol synthesis and RWGS pathways during CO2 hydrogenation; this discussion, however, must be prefaced by addressing complexities inherent for the analysis of reversible and interconnected reaction networks. Firstly, in a branched reaction network akin to that for CO2 hydrogenation, net rates of generation of stable species (e.g., CH3OH) generally differ from the net rates of reaction pathways (e.g., CO2 + 3H2 → CH3OH + H2O) as distinct pathways can lead to identical products (e.g., CO2 + 3H2 → CH3OH + H2O and CO + 2H2 → CH3OH both forming CH3OH). Despite of this, results from the preceding section demonstrate that the measured CH3OH rates under the conditions of this study stem predominantly from CO2 and that methanol dehydrogenation to CO is minimal, thus enabling us to write (10) r C H 3 O H ≈ R C O 2 → C H 3 O H where R C O 2 → C H 3 O H is the net rate of the CO2 to CH3OH (methanol synthesis) reaction pathway. Secondly, while measured thermodynamic quantities such as reversibility are instantaneous in a plug flow reactor, reaction rates measured at integral conversion represent site-time yields, which are inherently length-averaged values (Scheme 3 ). Formalisms and mathematical expressions relating reversibility and rates can therefore only be allayed if reversibility is consistently length-averaged, as illustrated by Razdan et al., or if instantaneous net rates (i.e., turnover frequencies (TOF)) are determined based on measured conversion, exemplified by the work of Franckaerts and Froment. We here evaluate instantaneous quantities and utilize the relationships (11a) R → C O 2 → C H 3 O H = R C O 2 → C H 3 O H 1 - Z e f f , C O 2 → C H 3 O H (11b) R ← C O 2 → C H 3 O H = R C O 2 → C H 3 O H Z e f f , C O 2 → C H 3 O H 1 - Z e f f , C O 2 → C H 3 O H which stem from the definition of effective reversibility, to determine the unidirectional forward and reverse rates. Furthermore, as discussed previously, effective reversibility of methanol synthesis can be equated with overall reversibility in this case to obtain (12a) R → C O 2 → C H 3 O H = R C O 2 → C H 3 O H 1 - Z o v , C O 2 → C H 3 O H (12b) R ← C O 2 → C H 3 O H = R C O 2 → C H 3 O H Z o v , C O 2 → C H 3 O H 1 - Z o v , C O 2 → C H 3 O H Analogous expressions can also be written for RWGS.

Following the approach of Franckaerts and Froment, the turnover frequencies for methanol synthesis and RWGS were determined by leveraging the characteristic equation for plug flow reactors and differentiating conversion ( X ) with respect to contact time ( τ ) (Eq. (13)). (13) R = dX d τ As illustrated in Fig. 5 a, conversions vary with contact time following the relationship given by (14) X = α τ 1 + β τ which was used to determine the trend lines shown via least-square fitting. Accordingly, the TOF at a given contact time can be expressed as (15) R = d d τ α τ 1 + β τ = α 1 + β τ - α β τ 1 + β τ 2 From there, the fitted conversion profiles were further utilized to calculate the partial pressure profile of each species; this, in turn, enables the determination of overall reversibility values at all contact times (Eq. (6); trend lines in Fig. 5b). These values are expectedly in good agreement with those determined from experimentally measured flow rates (data points in Fig. 5b). Eqs. (12) and (15), together with the values of overall reversibility, then provide a method to calculate instantaneous unidirectional forward and reverse rates for both methanol synthesis and RWGS (dashed and dotted lines in Fig. 5c). Data acquired at a 1:1 H2-to-CO2 ratio are shown in Fig. 5 as this led to the highest overall reversibility of methanol synthesis and, consequently, to net rates of methanol synthesis that are significantly convoluted by their forward and reverse components.

From Fig. 5c, the unidirectional reverse rates expectedly increase with increasing contact time and conversion as the system approaches equilibrium. On the other hand, the unidirectional forward rate of methanol synthesis surprisingly decreases more drastically with contact time than the unidirectional forward rate of RWGS, reflecting a difference in product inhibition rather than changes in reactant pressures as CO2 conversion only reached near 3 % despite Z o v , C O 2 → C H 3 O H ≈ 0.6 (Fig. 5b). These distinct behaviors of methanol synthesis and RWGS unidirectional forward rates, in turn, suggest that the two reactions (i) involve distinct intermediates and/or (ii) occur on different sites. At differential conversion and conditions far from equilibrium where net rates are a good approximation of the unidirectional forward rates, co-processing CO shows that CO inhibits methanol synthesis and RWGS rates only at pressures much higher than those present in the data shown in Fig. 5 (Fig. 6a). Furthermore, CO impacts both reactions equally such that the methanol selectivity is unchanged, making it unlikely the two reactions occur on different sites that are equally inhibited by CO. In contrast, co-processing H2O at differential and irreversible condition decreases the methanol selectivity, reflecting the trends in unidirectional forward rates shown in Fig. 5c and suggesting that methanol synthesis and RWGS involve distinct intermediates, with the intermediate for methanol synthesis more negatively impacted by H2O (Fig. 6b). This conclusion is consistent not only with the observed PH2 dependence (Fig. 2) and the purported branching reaction pathway (Scheme 2) but also with previously reported theoretical calculations and kinetic isotopic effect studies that proposed distinct intermediates for methanol synthesis and RWGS.

Implementing the above analysis at different feed compositions can further elucidate the effect of species concentrations on the forward and reverse unidirectional rates (Sec. S10; SI); specifically, we examine variations in H2 partial pressure as it is the only species with a non-unity stoichiometric coefficient (Eqs. (1) and (2)), consequently prescribing it a stronger influence on the reversibility of CO2 hydrogenation. As expected, the instantaneous turnover frequencies of methanol synthesis and RWGS extrapolated to zero conversion (equivalently the unidirectional forward rates) exhibit H2 dependencies consistent with those determined based on site-time yields measured at differential conversion and irreversible conditions (Figs. 2a and 7a). At nonzero CO2 conversions, the reactions are reversible, and Fig. 7 b shows that the unidirectional reverse rates of methanol synthesis (methanol dehydrogenation to CO2) and RWGS (WGS) are both inhibited by H2 at PCO2 = 4.7 bar and a CO2 conversion to CO of 0.02, a condition that ensures a constant CO partial pressure along with approximately constant CO2 and H2 partial pressures. While comparison of rates at constant species concentrations except for H2 is ideal, this is difficult to achieve as different H2 pressures lead to distinct product distributions at each contact time (Figs. 2 and 5c). Nonetheless, the decrease in unidirectional reverse rates shown in Fig. 7b should not stem from changes in PCH3OH and PH2O as increasing H2 partial pressure at a constant CO2 conversion to CO will lead to higher PCH3OH and PH2O since selectivity toward methanol increases with H2 partial pressure; as both CH3OH and H2O are reactants for the reverse reaction, increasing PCH3OH and PH2O is expected to increase rather than decrease the unidirectional reverse rates. Similar trends in the unidirectional reverse rates can also be observed at a constant CO2 conversion to methanol (constant methanol partial pressure) and a constant total CO2 conversion (constant H2O partial pressure) (Sec. S10; SI). The consistent decrease in unidirectional reverse rates with increasing PH2 for all three cases considered above reaffirms that H2 indeed inhibits the reverse reactions.

Our results thus show that both the forward and reverse unidirectional rates exhibit product inhibition. The unidirectional forward rate of methanol synthesis is first order in H2 partial pressure, but H2 inhibits the unidirectional reverse rate of methanol synthesis. Similarly, H2O is a reactant for the reverse reaction, yet it inhibits the unidirectional forward rate of methanol synthesis. While one might be tempted to rationalize these product inhibitions by leveraging Le Chatelier’s principle, it is crucial to recall that unidirectional rates, by definition, are devoid of any thermodynamic contributions. That is to say, the effects of reversibility and approach to equilibrium that form the basis of Le Chatelier’s principle have already been accounted for, and the observed product inhibition in Figs. 5c and 7b reflects intrinsic kinetic behaviors of the unidirectional forward and reverse rates of methanol synthesis and RWGS. In the following and final section, we demonstrate how these kinetic inferences can be applied in practice through polyfunctional catalysis.

The results obtained in the preceding sections detail a practical recipe based on kinetics to increase methanol yield and selectivity on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3: (i) increase H2 in the feed to selectively enhance the forward rate of methanol synthesis and (ii) remove the H2O product which preferentially inhibits the unidirectional forward rate of methanol synthesis. Regarding the former, data shown in Figs. 2 and 7a illustrate that increasing PH2 in the feed can enhance methanol selectivity to near 80 %. The second point then indicates that the use of a polyfunctional formulation incorporating a water adsorbent placed in intimate contact with catalyst particles should increase methanol production. Indeed, this enhancement was transiently observed using an interpellet mixture of Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 and molecular sieve 3A (Fig. 8 ; reaction-transport model shown in Sec. S11; SI). Adsorption of water on molecular sieve 3A resulted in a small delay in water evolution relative to the breakthrough of methanol and CO. This change in water evolution led to an enhancement in methanol yield and selectivity observed at approximately 1 ks of time-on-stream prior to saturation of the molecular sieve with H2O, after which rates and selectivity return to their steady-state values. Accordingly, the transient behavior can be reproduced through a pressure swing and temperature treatment at 523 K, which regenerates the molecular sieve (Sec. S12; SI). We stress that the reported enhancement in Fig. 8 was observed under irreversible conditions in contrast with typical sorption-enhanced reaction systems that leverage Le Chatelier’s principle to overcome equilibrium limitations, reflecting the alleviation of water inhibition for the unidirectional forward rate of methanol synthesis (Fig. 6b). Furthermore, the increase in methanol selectivity only manifests because H2O inhibits the unidirectional forward rates of methanol synthesis and RWGS differently. The use of a water adsorbent for product abstraction therefore not only alleviates thermodynamic limitations (equilibrium constraint) but also alleviates kinetic limitations (product inhibition) to increase the rate at which the system approaches equilibrium, in full accord with our kinetic analyses.

We provide, in this work, an assessment of methanol yield and selectivity during CO2 hydrogenation on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 based on reaction kinetics through in situ chemical titration, kinetic measurements under irreversible and reversible regimes, and mathematical formalisms leveraging the reversible nature of methanol synthesis and RWGS. Based on a constant Cl uptake across different H2:CO2 ratios, the active site density of Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 under working conditions was demonstrated to remain invariant with changing H2:CO2 ratio, ensuring that observed trends in rates reflect kinetic behaviors rather than changes in active site density. Measured reaction orders show that H2 and H2O serve as salient species governing methanol selectivity during CO2 hydrogenation on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 with H2 selectively enhancing and H2O preferentially inhibiting the methanol synthesis forward rate over the RWGS forward rate. The reversibility of methanol synthesis from CO2 is always higher than that of RWGS, proscribing sequential RWGS and CO hydrogenation as the mechanism for methanol production. CO2 hydrogenation instead occurs via a branched reaction network where both CO and methanol are derived from CO2 but through different intermediates, in accordance with the distinct influence of H2 and H2O on the unidirectional forward rates of the two reactions. H2 was further shown to inhibit the unidirectional reverse rates of both methanol synthesis and RWGS. Together, these results prescribe practical approaches to enhance methanol yield and selectivity from a kinetic standpoint: increasing PH2 by changing feed composition and decreasing PH2O by adding water adsorbents, both of which are demonstrated in this study. For simplicity of analysis, it is typical for kinetic studies to focus solely on conditions far from equilibrium where the net rate approaches the unidirectional forward rate as the reaction appears irreversible. The inclusion of integral reversibility data for reversible reaction systems, however, enables utilization of thermodynamic relationships to elicit additional mechanistic insights as shown for CO2 hydrogenation on Cu/ZnO/Al2O3.
